title: jn and the Cleft Sentence
short: jn + noun + participle stresses who did it: jn nsw rdj "it is the king who gives".
trouble: Students read this jn as a question. Before a noun and a participle, it singles out the doer.

blocks.html: jn asks questions (Questions) and means "by". Before a noun and a participle it has a third job: it points at the doer.

jn + noun + participle means "it is (noun) who does": jn nsw rdj ḥtp "it is the king who gives an offering". With a sḏm=f instead of a participle it refers to the future: jn nsw rdj=f n=k t "it is the king who will give you bread".

English singles out a doer with a "cleft" sentence: not "the king gives", but "it is the king who gives". Egyptian builds the same thing from pieces you know. The participle names the action ("one who gives", Active Participles), the noun names the doer, and jn marks the noun as the one meant, probably from its sense "by": "by the king (is) the giving". With a pronoun instead of a noun, Egyptian uses an independent pronoun (Independent Pronouns): ntf sḏm "it is he who hears".

opts.en: it is the god who hears my voice

blocks.cap: jn nṯr sḏm ḫrw=j: jn, the noun singled out, the participle, its object.

head: Egyptian
Translation
rows: it is the king who gives an offering
it is the god who hears my voice
it is his son who says the words
it was His Majesty who caused me to come
it is the king who will give you bread

blocks.title: Translate
steps: jn + noun zꜣ=f "his son" + participle ḏd "who says".
mdt "the words" is the participle's object.
blocks.a: "It is his son who says the words."

blocks.title: Write it
blocks.q: Write "It is the god who hears" with jn, nṯr and sḏm.
steps: jn, the noun nṯr, then the participle sḏm.

blocks.html: Why would a writer use it? To answer the question "who?". A king's inscription may insist that it was he, and no one else, who did a deed; a prayer may insist that it is this god who hears. When you see jn + noun + participle, the noun is the point of the sentence.

Reading this jn as a question. "Does the king give an offering?" would be jn dj nsw ḥtp, with jn before a full statement. Here jn is followed by a noun and then a participle, with no finite verb at all. Check what follows jn: a statement means a question; a noun plus a participle means "it is … who".
